rv.q: It’s gunning for something vast and the effect burrows its way into your body.
He brings outsider vibes to Oedipus – speaking in an elusive American drawl, adopting the mantle of leadership like a haunted robot.
Sadly though, alongside Indira Varma as his unsuspecting mum, Malek isn’t the best thing about Matthew Warchus’s apocalyptic staging.
But for all its stark physicality, this telling of the tale doesn’t reach into your core and rattle you with its painful, nagging questions about fate and human agency.
Varma’s is the performance of the evening.
I found the production too bizarre to hate, and there is something about it that works on a visceral level, if not a textual one.
In fact, it’s about six big pictures fudged together into a bewildering chaos.
Bursting with bold visuals and angsty, unsubtle performances, this ambitious, often incoherent take on Sophocles’ classic myth puts style firmly ahead of substance.
At the centre of it all is a curiously stilted central performance from Oscar winner Rami Malek.
This is in keeping with the project overall, which is a well-intended misfire.
Ultimately, this Oedipus is one for contemporary dance fans, and theatre lovers hoping for a coherent take on this often-told story should seek elsewhere.
It looks great but as a human drama, the discovery of the mother-son sexual relationship has almost no emotional impact.

For Malek is almost entirely at sea with Oedipus, his curious tic-ridden delivery strangling almost every word at birth, his American drawl soaked in a lazy grandiloquent insincerity, like an unholy blend of Trump at his most disingenuous and Biden at his most incoherent.
Invest in Warchus and Shechter’s gnomic bombasticism and you’ll glimpse beyond mere shock value.
This one lacks poetry but offers striking theatricality.

Overall, it’s a frustrating, uneven production, full of good ideas and powerful images, but ultimately dancing on the surface of Sophocles’s profoundly questing play, never quite piercing to its dark heart.
Malek is not that kind of actor.
In that respect, this is a very strong version of Oedipus albeit one with its own imperfections.
In this Oedipus, the performance is good, the dance is good, but they never fully come together, giving a disjointed feeling to the whole production.

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this visually striking but uneven production, with Shechter's choreography praised as the standout element while Malek's performance divides critics. Most agree it suffers in comparison to Icke's recent acclaimed version.
